source_refs.note: Chapter 9 exercise (PDF 208-211) solved: 12 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 13 short, 5 descriptive and 3 numerical questions with model answers. Book corrections: MCQ III, V, VI, X; Q.2(a), Q.2(e), Q.9.

blocks.prompt:
I. Given the following reaction:
NH₃(g) + H₂O(l) → NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

options.text: NH₃ is the acid, H₂O is the base
NH₃ is the base, H₂O is the acid
NH₄⁺ is the base, OH⁻ is the acid
H₂O is the base, OH⁻ is the acid

blocks.explanation: H₂O donates a proton (acid) and NH₃ accepts it (base); NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃ and OH⁻ the conjugate base of H₂O (9.1).

blocks.prompt: II. The pH of 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ of an aqueous solution of H₂SO₄ is:
blocks.explanation:
H₂SO₄ is a strong dibasic acid: each molecule gives 2H⁺.
[H⁺] = 2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
pH = −log(2 × 10⁻³) = 3 − 0.30 = 2.7

blocks.prompt: III. The solubility product of AgCl is 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻⁶. The maximum concentration of Ag⁺ ions in the solution is:
blocks.explanation:
AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); in a saturated solution [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = S
Ksp = S² = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰
S = √(2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.41 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The unit of Ksp for AgCl is printed as mol dm⁻⁶. Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻], so its unit is mol² dm⁻⁶.

blocks.prompt: IV. Which indicator is typically used for titrations involving strong acids and strong bases?
blocks.explanation: The pH jumps from about 4.0 to 10.0 at the end point of a strong acid-strong base titration, so phenolphthalein (range 8.2-10.0) can be used (9.9.2). Litmus is never used because its colour change is not sharp.

blocks.prompt: V. Which of the following is the conjugate base of water?
blocks.explanation: When water donates a proton it becomes OH⁻: H₂O → OH⁻ + H⁺. So OH⁻ is the conjugate base of water; H₃O⁺ is its conjugate acid (9.1).

blocks.prompt: Which of the following is a Lewis acid but not a Bronsted-Lowry acid?
blocks.explanation: AlCl₃ has no proton to donate, but its Al atom has an incomplete octet (like B in BF₃) and accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid only. HCl and H₂O are proton donors; NH₃ is a base (9.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Item V is printed as two questions under one numeral: the options of the first (conjugate base of water) are printed in one line without the label 'a.' before OH⁻(aq), and the second question (Lewis acid) has no number of its own. Both are solved here as printed.

blocks.prompt: VI. In an acid-base titration, the equivalence point is reached when:

options.text: Equal volumes of acid and base have been added.

blocks.explanation: The equivalence point is reached when the amount (moles) of base added is stoichiometrically equal to the amount of acid present (9.9.2). (a) is true only for strong acid-strong base; (b) is the end point.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: None of the printed options is exactly right. At the equivalence point the moles of acid and base are stoichiometrically equivalent (9.9.2); equal volumes are needed only when the two solutions have equal concentrations (for a 1:1 reaction). (a) pH 7.0 is true only for a strong acid–strong base titration, (b) the colour change marks the end point, which is only close to the equivalence point, and (d) the reaction does not simply 'stop'. (c) is keyed as the intended answer, reading 'equal volumes' as 'equivalent amounts (moles)'.

blocks.prompt: VII. If the concentration of Cl⁻ ion in a solution is increased, the solubility of silver chloride (AgCl) will:
blocks.explanation: Cl⁻ is a common ion: the ionic product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] exceeds Ksp, the equilibrium AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ shifts left and AgCl precipitates (common ion effect, 9.6). Solubility decreases but does not become zero.

blocks.prompt: VIII. Which of the following pairs of substances can act as a conjugate acid-base pair according to the Bronsted-Lowry theory?
blocks.explanation: A conjugate pair differs by one proton only: NH₄⁺ − H⁺ = NH₃ (9.1).

blocks.prompt: IX. If the pH of a solution is 11, what is the [OH⁻] concentration in the solution?
X. Which of the following pairs forms a buffer solution?
blocks.explanation: An acidic buffer is a weak acid with its salt with a strong base: CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa (9.7). HCl is a strong acid, NaOH + HCl just neutralise, and Na₂SO₄ is not a salt of NH₃.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (d) is printed without its closing bracket: 'sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄'. It should read sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄).

blocks.prompt: XI. What is the purpose of a titration acid-base curve?

options.text: To measure the volume of acid or base used
To determine the pH at various points during the titration
To calculate the concentration of the titrant
To identify the endpoint of the titration

blocks.explanation: A pH curve is a graph of pH against the volume of titrant added; it shows how pH changes during the titration and helps to choose the indicator (9.9.2).

blocks.prompt:
a. Define the following with an example for each:
i) Ionization constant
ii) Solubility product
ii) Common ion effect
iv) Acid-base Indicator
blocks.explanation:
i) Ionization constant (Ka): the equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak acid, Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; e.g. CH₃COOH, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.
ii) Solubility product (Ksp): the product of the molar concentrations of the ions in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt, each raised to its coefficient; e.g. PbSO₄, Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ at 25 °C.
iii) Common ion effect: suppression of the ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte with a common ion; e.g. NH₄Cl suppresses the ionization of NH₃ (NH₄OH).
iv) Acid-base indicator: a weak organic acid or base that changes colour to mark the end point; e.g. phenolphthalein, colourless in acid and pink-red in base (pH 8.2-10.0).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The third term is numbered 'ii)' a second time; it is iii) Common ion effect.

blocks.prompt:
b. Differentiate between:
i) Hydrolysis and dissolution
blocks.explanation: In dissolution a salt only breaks into ions in water; in hydrolysis those ions also react with water and change the pH.

rows: Ions of a salt react with water
Salt simply dissolves and separates into ions
Produces H₃O⁺ or OH⁻, so pH changes
No H₃O⁺ or OH⁻ formed, pH unchanged
Salts of a weak acid or weak base, e.g. NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺
e.g. NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); solution stays neutral

blocks.prompt: b. ii) Acidic and basic buffer solutions
blocks.explanation: Both resist a change in pH; they differ in what they are made of and in their pH.

rows: Weak acid + its salt with a strong base
Weak base + its salt with a strong acid
pH less than 7
pH more than 7
e.g. CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa (pH 4.74 at equal concentrations)
e.g. NH₄OH + NH₄Cl

blocks.prompt: c. Explain the concept of conjugate acid-base pairs. How are they related in terms of proton transfer?
blocks.explanation:
An acid that donates a proton becomes its conjugate base; a base that accepts a proton becomes its conjugate acid. The two members of a pair differ by one proton (H⁺).
HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻: pairs HCl/Cl⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O.

blocks.prompt: d. What is the relationship between the strength of an acid and the strength of its conjugate base?
blocks.explanation:
They are inversely related: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ is a very weak base (does not affect pH); CH₃COOH is a weak acid, so CH₃COO⁻ is a stronger base and hydrolyses to give OH⁻.

blocks.prompt:
e. For the following three reactions, identify the reactants that are Arrhenius bases, Bronsted-Lowry bases, and/or Lewis bases. State which type(s) of bases each reactant is. Explain your answers.
i) NaOH(s) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
i) HF(aq) + H₂O(l) → F⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
ii) H⁺(aq) + NH₃(aq) → NH₄⁺(aq)
blocks.explanation:
Reaction 1: NaOH is an Arrhenius base, because it gives OH⁻ ions in water.
Reaction 2: H₂O is a Bronsted-Lowry base (it accepts a proton from HF) and also a Lewis base (its O atom donates a lone pair to H⁺).
Reaction 3: NH₃ is a Bronsted-Lowry base (accepts H⁺) and a Lewis base (the lone pair on N forms a coordinate bond with H⁺).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The three reactions are numbered i), i), ii); they are reactions i), ii) and iii).

blocks.prompt:
f. An amphoteric substance can behave as either an acid or a base. Identify whether water behaves as an acid or a base in each of the following reactions.
i) H₂O + HCl → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻
ii) NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
iii) HNO₃ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + NO₃⁻
iv) CH₃COOH + H₂O ↔ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺
blocks.explanation:
i) Base: water accepts H⁺ from HCl and forms H₃O⁺.
ii) Acid: water donates H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻.
iii) Base: water accepts H⁺ from HNO₃.
iv) Base: water accepts H⁺ from CH₃COOH (a reversible reaction, ⇌).

blocks.prompt: g. Which salt would you expect to dissolve more readily in acidic solution: Barium sulfate or Barium fluoride? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Barium fluoride. F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF, so H⁺ removes it: H⁺ + F⁻ → HF. [F⁻] falls, the ionic product drops below Ksp and more BaF₂ dissolves (BaF₂(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺ + 2F⁻ shifts right).
SO₄²⁻ comes from the strong acid H₂SO₄ and is a very weak base, so acid hardly removes it and BaSO₄ stays insoluble.

blocks.prompt: h. Why does common ion effect decrease solubility of a less soluble salt?
blocks.explanation:
Adding a common ion raises the ionic product above Ksp. To keep Ksp constant the equilibrium shifts to the left and the salt precipitates, so less of it stays dissolved.
e.g. NaCl added to saturated AgCl: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ shifts left.

blocks.prompt: i. State the basic principle of solubility product. Mention factors affecting solubility product.
blocks.explanation:
Principle: in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt at a given temperature, the product of the ion concentrations (each raised to its coefficient) is constant, e.g. Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻].
Factors: Ksp depends on temperature and on the nature of the salt (and solvent). A common ion lowers the solubility of the salt, not its Ksp.

blocks.prompt: j. What is the main reason that titration of weak acids with weak bases are not performed for volumetric analysis?
blocks.explanation: Near the equivalence point the pH of a weak acid-weak base titration changes only gradually; there is no sharp jump. So no indicator gives a sharp colour change, and the end point cannot be detected accurately.

blocks.prompt: k. Prove by equations what happens when Na₂CrO₄ is added to saturated solution of PbCrO₄.
blocks.explanation:
PbCrO₄(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)
Na₂CrO₄(aq) → 2Na⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)
CrO₄²⁻ is the common ion; [Pb²⁺][CrO₄²⁻] becomes greater than Ksp, so Pb²⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq) → PbCrO₄(s). The equilibrium shifts left, PbCrO₄ precipitates and its solubility decreases (common ion effect).

blocks.prompt: l. According to the Lewis acid-base concept, Boron trifluoride (BF₃) can act as an acid. Is this statement correct?
blocks.explanation:
Yes. B in BF₃ has only six valence electrons (incomplete octet), so it accepts an electron pair from a Lewis base and forms a coordinate bond:
BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻ (also BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃).

blocks.prompt: m. If the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution is 1 × 10⁻⁵ M, what is the pH of the solution?
blocks.explanation:
Given: [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M
Formula: pH = −log[H⁺]
pH = −log(1 × 10⁻⁵)
pH = 5
The solution is acidic (pH < 7).

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Describe the Bronsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases. Provide examples of conjugate acid-base pairs and explain clearly their relationship.
blocks.explanation:
Theory (1923, Bronsted and Lowry): an acid is a species that donates a proton (H⁺) and a base is a species that accepts a proton in a proton-transfer reaction. It also works without water, which the Arrhenius theory cannot explain.
Examples:
1. HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq): HCl acid, H₂O base; pairs HCl/Cl⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O.
2. NH₃(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq): H₂O acid, NH₃ base; pairs NH₄⁺/NH₃ and H₂O/OH⁻.
3. HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s): proton transfer with no solvent and no OH⁻.
Other pairs (Table 9.1): HNO₃/NO₃⁻, H₂SO₄/HSO₄⁻, HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻.
Relationship: (i) the two members of a pair differ by one proton; (ii) acid − H⁺ = conjugate base and base + H⁺ = conjugate acid; (iii) the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base; (iv) water is amphoteric, a base towards HCl and an acid towards NH₃.

blocks.prompt: Q.4 Define the Lewis theory of acids and bases. How does this theory differ from the Bronsted-Lowry theory? Give examples of Lewis acids and bases that do not involve proton transfer.
blocks.explanation:
Lewis theory (1923, G.N. Lewis): a Lewis acid is any species that accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base is any species that donates an electron pair; the two form a coordinate covalent bond (an adduct).
Examples without proton transfer:
1. BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻ (BF₃ acid, incomplete octet; F⁻ base).
2. Ag⁺ + 2NH₃ → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Ag⁺ acid; each NH₃ donates its lone pair).
3. BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃; SO₃ + O²⁻ → SO₄²⁻; AlCl₃ is also a Lewis acid.

rows: Based on transfer of a proton (H⁺)
Based on an electron pair
Acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor
Acid = electron-pair acceptor, base = electron-pair donor
An acid must contain hydrogen
An acid need not contain hydrogen (BF₃, AlCl₃, Ag⁺)
Cannot explain BF₃ or Ag⁺ as acids
Wider: every Bronsted base is also a Lewis base

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Discuss applications and implications of the common ion effect in various fields.
blocks.explanation:
Common ion effect: adding a strong electrolyte with a common ion suppresses the ionization (or solubility) of a weak or sparingly soluble electrolyte.
Applications:
1. Purification of common salt: HCl gas passed through brine raises [Cl⁻]; [Na⁺][Cl⁻] exceeds its limit and pure NaCl crystallizes out.
2. Precipitating a less soluble salt: KCl added to a KClO₃ solution (common K⁺) makes KClO₃ settle down.
3. Salt analysis, group II: HCl (common H⁺) suppresses H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻, so the low [S²⁻] precipitates only group II sulfides.
4. Salt analysis, group III: NH₄Cl (common NH₄⁺) suppresses NH₄OH, so the low [OH⁻] precipitates only group III hydroxides.
5. Buffers: CH₃COONa suppresses CH₃COOH ionization (and NH₄Cl suppresses NH₄OH), giving solutions of nearly fixed pH; the body's blood buffer (bicarbonates) keeps blood pH steady.
Implications: a common ion always lowers the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt (AgCl in NaCl, PbCrO₄ in Na₂CrO₄) and shifts acid-base equilibria, which controls pH and precipitation.

blocks.prompt: Q.6 What is the solubility product for sparingly soluble salts. Give its two applications.
blocks.explanation:
Solubility product (Ksp): for a sparingly soluble salt in equilibrium with its saturated solution, e.g. PbSO₄(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq), the concentration of the solid is constant, so Kc[PbSO₄] = Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ at 25 °C. It is the product of the ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation (PbCl₂: Ksp = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]²). It is small and depends on temperature.
Application 1, solubility from Ksp: Ca(OH)₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻; Ksp = S(2S)² = 4S³ = 6.5 × 10⁻⁶, so S = 1.18 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³, [Ca²⁺] = 1.18 × 10⁻² and [OH⁻] = 2.36 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³.
Application 2, predicting precipitation: equal volumes of 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ Ca²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ of each; ionic product = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ > Ksp of CaSO₄ (2 × 10⁻⁵), so CaSO₄ precipitates. Ionic product > Ksp: precipitate; = Ksp: saturated; < Ksp: no precipitate.
(Also: common ion effect, e.g. Na₂CrO₄ precipitates PbCrO₄.)

blocks.prompt: Q.7 Describe the general shape of a titration curve for a strong acid titrated with a strong base. How can you identify the equivalence point on a titration curve for a strong acid-strong base titration?
blocks.explanation:
Shape (HCl titrated with NaOH; pH plotted against volume of NaOH added):
1. Start: only strong acid, fully dissociated; high [H⁺], so pH is very low.
2. Before equivalence: OH⁻ neutralises H⁺; pH rises slowly, the curve is nearly flat.
3. Near equivalence: a very steep, almost vertical rise in pH, from about 4.0 to 10.0, for a very small volume of base.
4. After equivalence: excess OH⁻; the curve flattens again at high pH.
Equivalence point: the moles of OH⁻ added equal the moles of H⁺ originally present. On the curve it is the middle of the steep vertical part, at pH 7.0 for a strong acid-strong base titration. An indicator changing colour inside the vertical part (phenolphthalein 8.2-10.0, or methyl orange) marks it as the end point.

blocks.prompt: Q.8 A buffer solution has a pH of 5.0. It is made from a weak acid HA with a pKa of 4.8. What is the ratio of the concentration of the conjugate base [A⁻] to the concentration of the weak acid [HA] in this buffer?
blocks.explanation:
Given: pH = 5.0, pKa = 4.8
Required: [A⁻]/[HA]
Henderson equation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
5.0 = 4.8 + log([A⁻]/[HA])
log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 5.0 − 4.8 = 0.2
[A⁻]/[HA] = antilog 0.2 = 10⁰·² = 1.58
Ratio [A⁻] : [HA] ≈ 1.6 : 1

blocks.prompt: Q.9 Calculate the solubility of a sparingly salt lead (II) iodide (PbI₂) in water. It has Ksp = 1.4 × 10⁻⁸.
blocks.explanation:
Given: Ksp of PbI₂ = 1.4 × 10⁻⁸
Required: molar solubility S
PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq)
At equilibrium: [Pb²⁺] = S, [I⁻] = 2S
Ksp = [Pb²⁺][I⁻]² = S × (2S)² = 4S³
4S³ = 1.4 × 10⁻⁸
S³ = 1.4 × 10⁻⁸ / 4 = 3.5 × 10⁻⁹
S = ∛(3.5 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.52 × 10⁻³
S = 1.5 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints 'a sparingly salt'; it should read 'a sparingly soluble salt'.

blocks.prompt: Q.10 The molar solubility of silver chromate (Ag₂CrO₄) in pure water at 298 K is 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Calculate the Ksp of silver chromate at this temperature.
blocks.explanation:
Given: S = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, T = 298 K
Required: Ksp
Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq)
[Ag⁺] = 2S = 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, [CrO₄²⁻] = S = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (2S)² × S = 4S³
Ksp = 4 × (6.5 × 10⁻⁵)³
Ksp = 4 × 2.746 × 10⁻¹³
Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹² mol³ dm⁻⁹
